items.originalTitle: ‘A savagely brutal map’: Senate GOP braces for 2028
items.author: Meredith Lee Hill
items.title: ‘A savagely brutal map’: Senate GOP braces for 2028
items.summary: Sen. Bernie Moreno isn’t sugarcoating things. The incoming chair of the National Republican Senatorial Committee will be in charge of defending 19 GOP seats in 2028 — and he’ll need to flip at least six more to regain control of the Senate majority. “Looking at it right now, it's absolutely a savagely brutal map,” the Ohio Republican said in an interview on Capitol Hill. After a historic midterms shellacking, Moreno is in the hot seat as he looks to navigate his chamber — and the party — through a rebuilding of its brand and its base over next two years. Republicans will likely have just 44 seats heading into 2028. They need to hold onto seats in battleground states like Wisconsin and North Carolina, while trying to flip seats held by Democratic Sens. Mark Kelly in Arizona, John Fetterman in Pennsylvania, Raphael Warnock in Georgia and Catherine Cortez Masto in Nevada. Moreno and his team have interviewed a handful of candidates over the last few days to be the next NRSC executive director, according to four people with direct knowledge of the matter, granted anonymity to discuss private conversations. Republicans expect Chris Grant, a former Moreno and Trump campaign staffer who now runs his own firm, to serve as a main outside GOP consultant for the committee. On top of the grueling map ahead, the Ohio Republican is facing the additional task of working with a lame duck president who still wields immense power over the GOP and its primaries. Then there’s the vice president, who is likely to run for president himself in the same two-year sprint. Moreno is close with both of those men. Asked how involved he expects the White House to be in GOP primaries and recruiting going forward, he replied, “We’re going to work on all of that.” It’ll be a complicated path forward. Moreno, over the past cycle has been unwilling to cast blame on President Donald Trump or Vice President JD Vance. Days before the midterm elections, he said if Republicans lost, it would be because people were “pissed off” about high gas prices. He’s unlikely to completely distance himself and the NRSC brand from the president's influence. But the party is currently undergoing a reckoning of how closely to align with the president after voters delivered an uncompromising rebuke of Trump’s economic agenda. Across the country, several battlegrounds and once-thought-to-be-safe red territory fell to Democratic hands. Trump in the 2026 cycle angered many Senate Republicans by supporting a primary challenge against Sen. John Cornyn of Texas — a move they privately say cost them north of $200 million as they tried, in vain, to save Ken Paxton’s imperiled campaign. The president also supported a primary challenge against Sen. Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, and pushed Sen. Thom Tillis to decide to retire in highly competitive North Carolina. One of the biggest challenges before Moreno and Senate Republicans after the midterms wipeout is to find candidates who can win a general election in highly competitive states, while also making it through GOP primaries where Trump will be a major factor. They’ll need to push back on the White House if the president tries, once again, to intervene — though that’s easier said than done. “There will be no patience for bad recruits this cycle,” said one senior Republican granted anonymity to discuss internal conversations, referring to the implosions of Paxton, Michael Whatley in North Carolina and other Republicans who were hand-picked by Trump. The White House referred POLITICO to Trump's post-midterms comments, where he blamed his party’s losses on the fact that he wasn’t on the ballot and said he brought several candidates "closer to victory," though they ultimately lost. Senate Majority Leader John Thune — who will be the minority leader next year — and his team plan to be heavily involved in recruitment efforts, according to two people involved in the conversations, granted anonymity to speak candidly. Their goal, one of the people said, is “to make sure we have our strongest possible candidates on the ballot in 2028.” Moreno is already trying to find a GOP recruit in his home state of Ohio to run against incoming Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown, whose term will be up again in 2028 after he won a special election against GOP Sen. Jon Husted earlier this month. The new NRSC chair said he’s looking for “somebody who can beat the crap out of Sherrod Brown.” Husted in private conversations hasn’t completely ruled out another bid, but he’s indicated he’s unlikely to run again, according to three people with knowledge of the matter, granted anonymity to speak candidly. Ohio Republicans expect former state Sen. Kevin Coughlin to explore a potential Senate bid. And they’re watching Rep. Mike Turner (R-Ohio), who just lost his reelection. Husted did not respond to a request for comment. A Turner spokesperson said in a statement that the representative "has been approached by several people about this and is keeping all his options open.” If Vance doesn’t seek his own presidential bid, Republicans in his home state are holding a long-shot hope that he, too, might consider a return to his old job. “JD Vance would be a dream candidate,” said one Ohio Republican. A version of this article first appeared in POLITICO Pro’s Morning Score . Want to receive the newsletter every weekday? Subscribe to POLITICO Pro . You’ll also receive daily policy news and other intelligence you need to act on the day’s biggest stories.

items.originalTitle: Poll: Most Americans think a Democrat will be the next president
items.author: Jason Beeferman
items.title: Poll: Most Americans think a Democrat will be the next president
items.summary: Nearly twice as many Americans expect a Democrat to win the presidency in 2028 than they do a Republican, a new POLITICO Poll finds . Even one in five of President Donald Trump’s own 2024 voters believe Republicans will lose the White House, a bad sign for the GOP as it struggles to recover from widespread losses this cycle and figure out its identity after spending a decade orbiting around Trump. Just 60% of Trump voters believe Republicans will keep the White House. Democratic voters are far more confident about their own party, according to the survey conducted by PF Global in the days after the midterm: Among voters who backed Kamala Harris, 87% expect Democrats to win in 2028. Beneath the unity is disagreement over what kind of nominee to pick. Pluralities of voters agree the next president should be a fighter when asked to choose from a list of qualities. But voters across the ideological spectrum also said they want other things from the country’s 48th president. While 43% of Harris voters want “a fighter,” 40% also selected “a progressive” and 34% chose “creative.” Among Trump voters, the 45% said they want to see “a conservative” elected president, surpassing the 39% who picked “a fighter.” They're also divided over what background their nominees should come from. Nearly three in 10 Trump voters say they would prefer the next president be someone who has not worked in Trump’s administration. That number rises to 46% among Trump voters who don’t identify as MAGA, whereas 82% of his loyal MAGA base would prefer the next president be someone who did work for Trump. That debate is playing out in real-time among top GOP leaders and lawmakers. More and more Hill Republicans are eyeing Secretary of State Marco Rubio for 2028, who they say is less associated with the midterm bloodbath than Vice President JD Vance. Others say the nominee should be someone entirely outside of Trump’s direct orbit. “As much as I like Rubio, and as much as I like Vance, they can't be our nominee,” said Dan McMaster, the chair of Michigan’s Shiawassee County Republican Party. “We need to get a Republican as far away from Trump as possible, and even then, I think it's going to be a battle.” “You've got to have some fresh blood in there, and you've got to have someone that has some distance from the crap that's gone on the last two years,” said one GOP strategist who worked on multiple House races last cycle and was granted anonymity to speak candidly about their own party. In a statement, Natalie Baldassarre, a spokesperson for the Republican National Committee, said the president isn’t going anywhere. "President Trump remains the unequivocal leader of our party who's cut taxes, lowered drug costs, and secured our border,” Baldassarre said. “Republicans will continue to harness his ability to energize our base and expose the Democrats' disastrous record to win in 2028." The White House also pointed POLITICO to separate polling earlier this month that shows Trump’s approval rating sits at 75% with all Republicans and jumps to 93% with those who identify as MAGA. “President Trump will never stop delivering results for the American people and he will undoubtedly go down as the most successful and consequential president in American history,” said Davis Ingle, a White House spokesperson. On election night earlier this month, Trump blamed his party’s losses on the fact that he wasn’t on the ballot, telling POLITICO by phone , “I wasn't on the ballot. If I was on the ballot, we would have won; we would have won it all very easily.” Meanwhile, Democrats have their own disagreements to figure out as they select their nominee. This cycle’s blue wave has bolstered the progressive wing of the party, which has long hoped to prove their candidates can win in purple battlegrounds, not just in safe-blue states. But the poll reveals skepticism remains — at least among moderates — over whether progressive wins in 2026 can translate to the presidential stage in 2028. The survey found a majority of progressive Democrats — 63% — want a progressive to be president, compared with just 23% of moderates who say the same. Half of progressive Democrats are convinced that being a progressive is a quality that will get their candidate elected in 2028. Moderates are less certain of that, though they’re also not as confident in their own faction: Just 37% think being a moderate is a quality that ensures the Democratic candidate wins. “Whoever's running for president has seen what's happened and also has seen the power of our movement, and so this is something that could be carried on to 2028,” said progressive New Jersey Democratic Rep.-elect Adam Hamawy, reflecting on the wins he and others enjoyed this cycle. “Despite it being the most expensive elections in history, we showed that people are able to beat out money when we come together.” And with Democrats winning Senate seats in deep-red states like Kansas and Mississippi for the first time in decades, many now argue that the entire map is in play for 2028. The poll found that 60% of Democrats think the party should focus their efforts on winning all states in the presidential election, even ones that seemed like deep Republican areas, rather than focus on holding the states where they know their supporters are. Republicans felt the same, with 56% also arguing for an “all states” approach as the party races to rebuild in territory they once thought was safe. “I have been very, very loud about the fact that the path to the presidency leads through the South,” said Democratic strategist Dallas Jones, who ran statewide Black voter engagement for Lone Star Rising PAC, the outside group that supported Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico. “But again, we don't make investments there. items.originalTitle: Build a Personal Brand to Help Employers Find You
items.author: Brian Jenney
items.title: Build a Personal Brand to Help Employers Find You
items.summary: This article is crossposted from IEEE Spectrum ’s careers newsletter. Sign up now to get insider tips, expert advice, and practical strategies, written i n partnership with tech career development company Parsity and delivered to your inbox for free! In one year, the number of developers working for themselves has more than doubled. Stack Overflow’s annual survey of more than 30,000 developers showed that freelancers and sole proprietors went from about four percent of respondents to ten percent. You can read this as a polite way of saying, “ I got laid off and I’m figuring it out.” But I don’t think the number can be ignored. Whatever the case, it leads to the question I keep hearing from engineers right now: What can I do to stay employable? One tried and true answer is to build a personal brand. But what does that actually mean? Over the last six years, I grew my LinkedIn audience to 40,000 followers and YouTube channel to 10,000. I don’t think you should aim to be famous (unless you’re into that sort of thing) but I do think it’s worth exploring how to be discoverable online in 2027 if you want an advantage in the open market. A personal brand is a discovery mechanism Strip away the follower counts and the AI-generated thought leadership, and a personal brand comes down to a simple question: Does the internet know who you are? When a hiring manager goes looking for someone who has your skills, do you show up? You can think of this as search engine optimization for your employability. Recruiters have mostly consolidated around a single platform to find people: LinkedIn. Those 40,000 followers and millions of impressions came with barely a viral post to my name. Nobody is begging me to do sponsorships. But I rarely have trouble finding work, and far more opportunities come to me than I go looking for. That has much less to do with fame than with being easy to find. You don’t need 10,000 followers. You need a trail of breadcrumbs. Don’t write AI slop LinkedIn is notorious for being overrun with AI-generated posts. It’s become a running joke. That’s good news for you, because the bar to stand out is “sound like a human being.” Write about what you actually achieved: a hairy bug you squashed, how your team handles deployments, why you picked some obscure library, the migration that went sideways at 2 a.m. Specifics are hard to fake and easy to trust. (But be careful not to post sensitive information.) And post a picture of yourself once in a while. People connect with faces a lot faster than with walls of text. Hot takes, with caution Posts with an opinion tend to outperform tutorials, but you don’t have to dunk on anyone to have one. For instance, if you work on a tech stack people love to mock (VB, .NET, some ancient Java monolith held together with prayer), try something like “What people get wrong about .NET.” You’ll attract a few trolls in the comments—free engagement, honestly—plus people who want an actual conversation. These comments can turn into actual connections and even… friends. A routine you can follow Posting twice a week is not a big ask. Pick a simple, repeatable format so you’re never staring at an empty text box: what you worked on, what broke, and what you learned. Even a post that gets 10 views leaves one more breadcrumb about who you are and what you know. Over time, the people who comment become your network. And because so few engineers post about their work on LinkedIn, you can become a big fish in a small pond surprisingly fast. Write for the people a few steps behind you The best audience is engineers one or two steps behind where you are now. Answer the questions you had a year ago. It helps them, it sharpens your own thinking, and every so often it turns into mentorship in both directions. It also tells a future employer more about how you think than any résumé bullet ever could. The engineers who grab the most opportunities are the ones employers can find. You don’t need to become an influencer to be one of them. You just need to leave enough breadcrumbs that the right person can follow them back to you. —Brian IEEE Xplore Digital Library Adds AI Assistant To help researchers search through the millions of peer-review publications in the IEEE Xplore Digital Library, IEEE has released a custom AI suite optimized for STEM literature. The suit allows users to search with natural-language queries and provides overviews with reference links. Read more here . Systems Thinking Is Vital in the Age of AI AI has made it easier to access information in different domains, but specialist knowledge and human judgement still serve an essential role. Today, an engineer’s core value comes from knowing how to ask the right questions—not from knowing everything. Read more here .
